entry: Period in the history of Western philosophy, beginning in the early 20th century. It was shaped by the increasing professionalization of the discipline, which took hold first in Germany; in the United States it grew out of higher-education reforms based largely on the German model. Two rival traditions emerged. [[Analytic philosophy]] emphasizes logical precision, linguistic clarification and alignment with empirical science, and its work in formal logic owes much to [[Bertrand Russell]]. Continental philosophy emphasizes phenomenological description and historical interpretation, and developed [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and critical theory; [[Martin Heidegger]] is a central figure. The term is often confused with modern philosophy, an earlier period, and with postmodern philosophy, a critique of modern philosophy.

Submerged, gently sloping margin of a [[Continent|continent]], extending seaward from the shore to the shelf break. Much of the shelf was exposed by drops in [[Sea level|sea level]] during glacial periods. It is covered largely by terrigenous [[Sediment|sediment]] eroded from the land, and its width varies considerably. With few exceptions, the shelf break, where the steeper continental slope begins, lies at a remarkably uniform depth of roughly 140 m (460 ft). Continental shelves cover about 27 million sq km (10 million sq mi), roughly 7% of the ocean surface area. The largest, the Siberian Shelf in the [[Arctic Ocean|Arctic Ocean]], stretches 1,500 km (930 mi) in width, and the [[South China Sea]] lies over the Sunda Shelf. Under the [[United Nations]] Convention on the Law of the Sea, the continental shelf is legally defined as the seabed adjacent to the shores of a country to which it belongs.

Mathematical function with no abrupt changes in value. A function is continuous if small changes in its argument produce at most small changes in its value, so that its graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Continuity is one of the core concepts of [[Calculus|calculus]] and [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]]. Formally, a function is continuous at a point when the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of the function there equals its value. Until the 19th century mathematicians relied largely on intuitive notions of continuity, and the epsilon–delta definition of a limit was introduced to formalize it. The concept has been generalized to functions between [[Metric space|metric spaces]] and [[Topological space|topological spaces]], the latter forming the basis of [[Topology|topology]]. The height of a growing flower over time is continuous, whereas the money in a bank account jumps at each deposit or withdrawal and is discontinuous. All [[Polynomial|polynomial]] functions are continuous everywhere.

Family of symmetric probability distributions on a bounded interval. Also called the rectangular distribution and often written U(a, b), it describes an outcome lying between a minimum a and a maximum b. Every interval of equal length within the bounds is equally probable. The [[Probability density function|density]] is 1/(b − a) across the interval, so its graph is a rectangle. It is the maximum entropy distribution for a [[Random variable|random variable]] with no constraint other than its support.

Branch of mechanics treating materials as continuous media rather than collections of discrete particles. It deals with deformable bodies and with the transmission of forces through them. The model assumes that the substance completely fills the space it occupies, which gives an accurate description at length scales much greater than interatomic distances. Behavior is described by [[Differential equation|differential equations]] expressing conservation of mass, momentum and energy, together with material-specific constitutive relationships. Physical properties are represented by [[Tensor|tensors]], whose form does not depend on the coordinate system chosen. The theories of [[Elasticity (physics)|elasticity]], [[Plasticity (physics)|plasticity]] and [[Fluid mechanics|fluid mechanics]] rest on its concepts.

Trick-taking [[Card game|card game]] for four players in two partnerships, played with a standard 52-card deck. Partners sit opposite each other. Each deal passes through an auction in which the players bid to take the contract, specifying how many tricks the declaring side must win. Partners use their bids to exchange information about their hands, and no other means of conveying information is permitted. The game descended from whist through *Biritch*, a 19th-century game; the first known rule book, dated 1886, was written by an English financier working in [[Constantinople]]. Another theory holds that British soldiers in the [[Crimean War]] invented bridge. Rubber bridge is the most popular casual form, while most club and tournament play uses duplicate bridge, in which the same deal is played at several tables for comparative scoring.

Legally enforceable agreement creating rights and obligations between two or more parties. A contract typically involves consent to transfer [[Goods|goods]], services or [[Money|money]], or a promise to do so at a future date. If one party breaches a contract, the injured party may seek [[Damages|damages]] or equitable remedies such as specific performance or rescission. Contract law rests on the principle that agreements must be honored, and it varies between [[Common law|common law]], [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] and mixed jurisdictions. Common law jurisdictions typically require consideration for a contract to be valid, whereas civil law jurisdictions require only a meeting of the minds. Civil law systems based on the [[Napoleonic Code]] distinguish systematically between types of contract. The UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts, published in 2016, reject the doctrine of consideration. Contract law is distinct from [[Tort|tort]] law, which deals with civil wrongs between parties not already in a legal relationship.

Logical incompatibility of a [[Proposition|proposition]] with itself, with established [[Fact|fact]], or with another proposition. The law of noncontradiction holds that a thing cannot both belong and not belong to the same object at the same time and in the same respect. It is often used as a tool to detect disingenuous [[Belief|beliefs]] and [[Bias|bias]]. In modern formal logic, a contradiction is a proposition from which falsity can be derived, denoted by the falsum symbol ⊥. In classical logic any proposition can then be proved, a principle called ex falso quodlibet, or explosion. Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of a claim and derives a contradiction; a classic example is the proof that √2 is irrational. [[Plato]]'s Euthydemus dialogue uses a paradox to demonstrate the need for the notion of contradiction.

headword: Control of fire by early humans
sort_key: control of fire by early humans
entry: Prehistoric technology critical to human evolution. Fire provided warmth and light, protection from predators, a means of making hunting tools and a method of cooking food, enabling humans to disperse geographically and to change their diet and behavior. Claims of fire use by a member of [[Homo|Homo]] reach as far back as 2.0 million years ago, and human use of fire is documented 1.79 million years ago in Wonderwerk Cave, [[South Africa|South Africa]]. Microscopic wood ash is accepted as evidence of fire use by [[Homo erectus|Homo erectus]] from about 1 million years ago. The oldest likely evidence of cooking, fish teeth heated deep in a cave at the Daughters of Jacob Bridge in the Golan Heights, dates to about 780,000 years ago. The oldest definitive evidence of fire-making, from a [[Neanderthal|Neanderthal]] site in eastern England, dates to about 400,000 years ago. Controlled fire becomes far more widespread 400–300,000 years ago, and nearly universal among [[Early modern human|anatomically modern humans]] around 125–120,000 years ago.

Branch of engineering and applied mathematics dealing with the control of [[Dynamical system|dynamical systems]]. It seeks a model or algorithm that applies system inputs to drive a system to a desired state, minimizing delay, overshoot and steady-state error while keeping the system stable. A controller compares the controlled process variable with a set point, and the resulting error is fed back to generate a corrective action. Control theory underlies the automation that revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft and communications and created [[Robotics|robotics]]. Formal analysis began in 1868, when [[James Clerk Maxwell|James Clerk Maxwell]] analyzed the centrifugal governor. Stability criteria were contributed by Edward Routh and Adolf Hurwitz, and PID control was developed from 1922 by Nicolas Minorsky. As the general theory of feedback systems, control theory is useful in [[Economics|economics]], [[Operations research|operations research]] and the life sciences.

Highway designed for high-speed traffic, with all ingress and egress regulated. Common terms include freeway, motorway and expressway. A fully controlled-access highway has no traffic signals, intersections or property access; crossing roads and railways pass over or under it, and slip roads at interchanges provide entry and exit. A median separates opposing directions, which improves safety while raising capacity and speed. These highways evolved in the first half of the 20th century. [[Italy|Italy]] opened the first, the autostrada A8 between [[Milan|Milan]] and Varese, in 1924. In 1932 [[Germany|Germany]] completed the first controlled-access autobahn without speed limits, between [[Cologne|Cologne]] and [[Bonn|Bonn]]. The first North American freeways, known as parkways, opened in the [[New York City|New York City]] area in the 1920s. Britain did not build its first motorway until 1958.

Movement of a fluid driven by differences in its properties, especially [[Density|density]], together with body forces. In thermodynamics the term often refers to [[Heat transfer|heat transfer]] by convection. In natural convection, [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]] makes less dense fluid rise and denser fluid sink, and the density contrasts usually arise from differences in temperature or composition. Convection is common in the atmosphere and [[Ocean|oceans]], and it occurs in [[Earth's mantle|Earth's mantle]], in [[Star|stars]] and in some solid materials such as ice. It is important in ventilation, cooling and [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]]. Whether natural convection develops depends on the relative effects of buoyancy, [[Viscosity|viscosity]] and diffusion, described by dimensionless numbers such as the Rayleigh number. Convective motion often organizes into convection cells.

Informal, interactive [[Communication|communication]] between two or more people. Conversational skills and [[Etiquette|etiquette]] are an important part of socialization, and conversational ability in a new language is a frequent focus of language teaching. No generally accepted definition exists beyond the involvement of at least two people, so the term is often defined by what it is not. A ritualized exchange such as a mutual [[Greeting|greeting]] is not a conversation, nor is an interaction with a marked status differential, such as a boss giving orders. Conversation is generally face to face and synchronous, unlike asynchronous written messages. Conversations follow rules derived from the cooperative principle, and each contribution responds to what has been said. One estimate suggests that 85% of face-to-face communication is nonverbal. Conversation analysis, a branch of sociology, studies the structure and organization of human interaction.

Geometric set containing every line segment between any two of its points. A solid cube is convex, but a hollow figure or a crescent shape is not. The [[Mathematical optimization|convex hull]] of a set is the smallest convex set containing it. A convex function is one whose epigraph, the set of points on or above its graph, is a convex set. Convex minimization, a subfield of optimization, studies minimizing convex functions over convex sets, and convex analysis studies their properties. The convex subsets of the [[Real number|real numbers]] are intervals and points. Solid regular [[Polygon|polygons]] and [[Triangle|triangles]] are convex in the plane, and the [[Platonic solid|Platonic solids]] are convex in three dimensions. The Kepler–Poinsot polyhedra are not.

Integral operation on two functions that measures the overlap of one as it is shifted across the other. The convolution f∗g is the integral of the product of the two functions after one is reflected about the y-axis and shifted. The result does not depend on which function is reflected. Convolution is used in [[Signal processing|signal processing]], image processing, probability, statistics and physics. The [[Fourier transform|Fourier transform]] converts convolution into pointwise multiplication, which enables fast computation. Computing the inverse of convolution is called deconvolution.

Zero-player cellular automaton devised by British mathematician John Horton Conway in 1970. Each cell of an infinite square grid is live or dead, and all cells update together according to their eight neighbors: a live cell with two or three live neighbors survives, and a dead cell with exactly three becomes live. Patterns include still lifes, oscillators and spaceships. The game is Turing complete and can simulate any [[Turing machine|Turing machine]].

Self-governing island country in free association with [[New Zealand|New Zealand]], in [[Polynesia|Polynesia]], South [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] (pop., 2021: 14,987). It consists of 15 islands with a total land area of about 236.7 sq km (91 sq mi) and an exclusive economic zone of 1,960,027 sq km (756,771 sq mi). The capital is Avarua, on Rarotonga, the most populous island. The islands were first settled around AD 1000 by Polynesians thought to have migrated from [[Tahiti|Tahiti]]. They were named after [[James Cook|James Cook]], who visited in the 1770s. Most Cook Islanders hold New Zealand citizenship. Since the start of the 21st century the country has conducted its own foreign and defence policy. Tourism is the leading element of the economy, with over 168,000 visitors in 2018.

Strait separating the [[North Island|North Island]] and [[South Island|South Island]] of New Zealand. It connects the [[Tasman Sea|Tasman Sea]] to the northwest with the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]] to the southeast, and at its narrowest point it is 22 km (14 mi) wide. It has been described as "one of the most dangerous and unpredictable waters in the world." The strait is named after [[James Cook|James Cook]], the first European commander to sail through it, in 1770. Strong tidal flows dominate its waters, and many ships have been wrecked there, including the Maria in 1851 and the TEV Wahine in 1968. Regular ferries run between Picton and [[Wellington|Wellington]]. [[Abel Tasman|Abel Tasman]], who first saw New Zealand in 1642, thought the strait was a bight closed to the east. Its Māori name is *Te Moana-o-Raukawa*.

Starchy [[Banana|banana]] cultivar, generally cooked rather than eaten raw. Many cooking bananas are called plantains, though botanically the term refers only to true plantains of the AAB group. Cooking bananas are hybrids of *Musa acuminata* and *Musa balbisiana*. They have more [[Starch|starch]] and less sugar than dessert bananas, and green plantains are typically boiled or fried. Dried and processed, they become flour for cakes, bread and pancakes. Plantains are a staple food in tropical regions, ranking as the 10th most important staple food in the world. In Africa they provide more than 25 percent of the calories needed by over 70 million people. An average plantain provides about 920 kilojoules (220 kilocalories) of food energy and is a good source of [[Potassium|potassium]] and dietary fiber.

Plant or animal liquid fat used in frying, [[Baking|baking]] and other cooking. Oil allows higher cooking temperatures than water, cooking food faster and more evenly, and it can impart its own flavor. Plant oils include olive, palm, soybean, [[Rapeseed|canola]], corn, peanut, sesame and sunflower oil; animal oils include [[Butter|butter]], ghee, schmaltz and [[Lard|lard]]. Coconut, palm and palm kernel oils contain much saturated fat and are solid at room temperature. Meta-analyses link high saturated fat consumption to higher blood LDL cholesterol, a risk factor for [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]]. Trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils raise the risk of coronary heart disease, and in the U.S. they cannot be added to foods, including cooking oils, without special permission. Oils rich in unsaturated [[Fatty acid|fatty acids]] oxidize more rapidly when heated, so the oil should match the cooking temperature.

Food preparation equipment, such as pots, frying pans and baking sheets, used in kitchens. Cookware is used on a stove or cooktop and bakeware in an [[Oven|oven]], and some items serve both. Materials differ in heat conduction and retention: [[Copper|copper]] conducts heat well, [[Cast iron|cast iron]] retains it but must be seasoned, and [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] resists corrosion. Handles and knobs of [[Bakelite|Bakelite]], plastic or wood stay cool enough to grip without oven gloves. The earliest known pottery vessels, dating from 19,600 ± 400 years before present, were found in Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi, China. Before pottery, people boiled water by dropping heated stones into vessels such as turtle shells or leaf-lined pits, and [[Bamboo|bamboo]] tubes sealed with clay served as containers in Asia.

Device for rejecting waste heat to the atmosphere by cooling a circulating water stream. Most cooling towers use [[Evaporation|evaporation]] to cool water close to the wet-bulb air temperature; dry cooling towers rely on air and radiators alone. Common applications include cooling water in [[Petrochemical|petrochemical]] and [[Chemical plant|chemical plants]], oil refineries, [[Power station|thermal power stations]], nuclear power stations and HVAC systems. The largest hyperboloid towers can be up to 200 m (660 ft) tall and 100 m (330 ft) in diameter, while most are much smaller units on buildings. Their emissions consist solely of [[Water vapor|water vapor]]. Cooling towers originated in the 19th century with condensers for [[Steam engine|steam engines]]. Dutch engineers Frederik van Iterson and Gerard Kuypers patented the hyperboloid design on August 16, 1916. Warm towers can harbor Legionella bacteria, linked to [[Legionnaires' disease|Legionnaires' disease]], so they require disinfection and monitoring.

Joint action by a group of [[Organism|organisms]] for collective benefit rather than [[Competition|competition]] for individual gain. In biology, many [[Animal|animal]] and [[Plant|plant]] [[Species|species]] cooperate with members of their own species and with other species in symbiotic or mutualistic relationships. Many organisms, including fish, birds and insects, show cooperative behavior such as teaching, helping and self-sacrifice. Humans cooperate for reasons shared with other animals, such as immediate benefit, genetic relatedness and reciprocity, and also through honesty signaling, indirect reciprocity and cultural group selection. Language allows cooperation on a very large scale. In one experiment, 19 people were scanned by MRI while playing an ultimatum game as responders. They rejected unfair offers from human partners at a significantly higher rate than from a computer partner, and the refusals were associated with negative [[Emotion|emotions]] generated in the anterior insula.

Method of using one or more numbers, or coordinates, to determine uniquely the position of points or other geometric elements on a manifold such as [[Euclidean space|Euclidean space]]. Coordinates are usually real numbers, but may be complex numbers or elements of a commutative ring. The simplest system is the number line, on which each point's coordinate is its signed distance from an origin. The [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian system]] uses perpendicular axes in the plane and three mutually orthogonal planes in space, generalizing to n coordinates in n-dimensional space. Polar coordinates use a pole and an angle, and cylindrical and [[Spherical coordinate system|spherical coordinates]] extend them to three dimensions. Translating problems in geometry into problems about numbers is the basis of [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]].

Primary time standard used worldwide to regulate clocks and set civil time. UTC is based on International Atomic Time (TAI), a weighted average of hundreds of [[Atomic clock|atomic clocks]] worldwide. It stays within about one second of mean solar time at 0° longitude, the [[Prime meridian|prime meridian]], and it is not adjusted for [[Daylight saving time|daylight saving time]]. It is the effective successor to [[Greenwich Mean Time|Greenwich Mean Time]] in everyday use. Coordinated time signals began on January 1, 1960, and UTC was first officially adopted as a standard in 1963. Leap seconds were added several times from 1972 to 2016. In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures resolved to end leap seconds by 2035, and a 2026 resolution calls for continuous UTC from May 20, 2027.
